title: Ninety Days
passage:
The lost-property office behind the bus station keeps what it is handed for ninety days. Clothing then goes to a charity shop, phones and cameras to a saleroom, and the umbrellas – there are always umbrellas – into a bin bag that somebody carries out to the yard. An umbrella is worth less than the fare back into town to collect it, and anyone who has left one on the number 14 works that out somewhere around the second stop. ___(1)___, the umbrella rack is cleared twice a year and the rest of the room once. Every item gets a paper tag with the date, the route and the name of whoever handed it in. By the time that tag is filled out, the owner has usually ___(2)___ it up for lost.

The claiming end of the business is looser than any of that suggests. No one is asked for a receipt or a crime number. Whoever turns up describes the thing, and if the description matches the tag, the office takes them at their ___(3)___ and the coat goes back across the counter. Two questions is the usual limit, and the second one is often about a pocket. Under that same counter, though, there is a locked drawer, and anything worth more than about fifty pounds goes into it: a laptop, a passport, a ring in a paper envelope. Everywhere else in the room a description is enough. At the drawer it is not, and the questions asked there are ___(4)___.

Whether the drawer contradicts the room, or is the reason the room can afford to work as it does, is not something anyone behind the counter has needed to settle. An umbrella’s future is a foregone ___(5)___ before the ink is dry; a set of keys is another matter. Keys are kept past the ninety days, in a tin, because nobody there can quite bring themselves to throw away a stranger’s front door. The finder’s name is written on every tag in full, in a box about the size of a stamp. Nobody has ever come back to ask for it.
– Georgina Chalkwright writes about civic life for a regional weekly.

questions.rationale: Connective gap. All four options are formal sentence-initial adverbs of the same epistemic-evaluative class, all in -ly and two of them in -ably, so register and shape separate nothing. The sentence before the gap sets out a piece of everyday arithmetic: an umbrella is worth less than the fare back into town, and the person who left it has worked that out before the bus has gone two stops. The gapped sentence reports the operational consequence - the umbrella rack is cleared twice a year and the rest of the room once. Umbrellas come in and are never fetched, so their shelf fills faster than any other; the second clause is exactly what the first clause leads a reader to expect, which is what 'Predictably' asserts. It locks. Conversely = wrong_logic: it demands that the second statement invert the first, and clearing the rack more often than the room is the outcome of the arithmetic, not its opposite; a solver who has half-registered the concessive feel of 'worth less than' may still reach for it. Arguably = wrong_logic and the deliberate hedge trap: it frames what follows as a contestable claim, but a clearing schedule is a plain operational fact stated by an observer, not a proposition anyone could argue about - and, for the hedge audit, this puts the cautious-sounding option in the wrong column. Ostensibly = wrong_logic: it posits a gap between what is claimed and what is really so, and the passage offers no such gap - nothing suggests the rack is only supposedly cleared twice a year.

Collocation gap. All four options are bare past participles of common verbs that take particles, so the set is POS-uniform and every member looks equally at home in a phrasal-verb frame. The frame is 'the owner has usually ___ it up for lost', and English has exactly one idiom that fits the whole string: to give something up for lost. The surrounding sense supports it - the tag is being written while the owner has already stopped expecting the thing back. 'given' locks. written = collocation_misfit and the strongest lure, because 'written it off as lost' is a real and very close idiom; but 'write up' means to compose a report, and 'written it up for lost' has no reading. put = collocation_misfit, lured by 'put it down as lost', which is also real; 'put it up for' takes sale or auction, not a state of loss. counted = collocation_misfit, lured by 'counted it as lost' and by 'count up'; the latter means to tally, and 'counted it up for lost' is not English. Only 'given' completes the idiom the particle demands.

Collocation gap. All four options are short nouns from the vocabulary of credibility, which is the field the whole paragraph is working in, so every one of them is thematically flattering and none is separable on register. The frame is 'the office takes them at their ___', and the fixed English idiom for accepting what somebody says without further evidence is to take someone at their word. The clause before it supplies the sense exactly - a description is offered, it matches the tag, and the coat is handed over. 'word' locks. face = collocation_misfit and the sharpest lure, because 'take it at face value' is a real idiom about accepting something as it presents itself, which is precisely what the office is doing; but the idiom is fixed on 'value' and cannot be split, and 'at their face' is not English. honour = collocation_misfit: 'on their honour' and 'word of honour' both exist and both belong to this exact semantic field, yet 'takes them at their honour' has no reading. trust = surface_word_match: it is the abstraction the passage is circling, so a skimmer reaches for it on theme alone, but one takes a thing on trust, never someone at their trust. Only 'word' completes the idiom.

Polarity gap. All four options are -ing adjectives of similar length and register describing manner towards another person, so shape gives no purchase at all. The frame is contrastive and the contrast is stated twice: 'Everywhere else in the room a description is enough. At the drawer it is not, and the questions asked there are ___.' The 'it is not' forces the negative pole - whatever is true of questions at the drawer must be the opposite of easily satisfied - and English supplies the collocation for it, a searching question. The drawer's contents (a laptop, a passport, a ring) supply the reason. 'searching' locks. forgiving = polarity_mirror and the designed trap: it sits at the lenient pole that the frame has just ruled out, and it is close enough to a real collocation (a forgiving surface, a forgiving examiner) to feel available to a solver who has skimmed past the 'it is not'. obliging = polarity and sense misfit: it names a positive-pole social manner and it is predicable of a person, not of a question, so 'obliging questions' collocates with nothing. reassuring = polarity_mirror at second remove: a reassuring question would soothe the claimant, whereas the drawer exists in order to test one, and nothing in the paragraph asks the office to comfort anybody. Note for the hedge audit: the key here is the strict, unsoftened option and all three softer options are wrong, so the test-wise habit of choosing the mild answer scores zero on this gap.

Collocation gap. All four options are abstract -ion nouns of settled outcomes, fully suffix-rhymed and close in register, so nothing separates them on form. The frame is 'An umbrella’s future is a foregone ___ before the ink is dry', and 'foregone' is a defective adjective in modern English: it collocates with exactly one noun. The passage has already earned the sense - umbrellas are never fetched and go out in a bin bag - so what is being asserted is that the ending is settled in advance. 'conclusion' locks. decision = collocation_misfit and the most plausible lure, since a decision is the outcome of the semantic field 'foregone' points at and the phrase 'a foregone decision' is the kind of thing a non-native ear will accept; it simply does not exist in English. resolution = collocation_misfit: right suffix, right family of endings-and-outcomes, and available in the sense of a matter being resolved, yet 'a foregone resolution' collocates with nothing. conviction = collocation_misfit with an extra pull, because its legal sense sits near the courtroom register in which 'foregone conclusion' is most often heard; 'a foregone conviction' is still not English. Only 'conclusion' takes this adjective.
